title: Hollywood Ending
full_review:
A has-been director is given another chance, only to allow his hypochondriacal tendencies to get in his way in the disappointing comedy "Hollywood Ending" (DreamWorks).

Writer-director Woody Allen's latest film starts off promisingly, and even ends on a pretty funny joke made at the expense of French movie audiences. But the central conceit of the film -- that an aging auteur goes psychosomatically blind and must keep it a secret from everyone involved in the film he's directing -- wears thin all too soon. It turns the bulk of the movie into a flat, overlong jumble dotted with occasionally humorous moments. And several of the inside industry jokes Allen makes may go over the heads of an average audience unfamiliar with intricacies or lingo of studio filmmaking.

To a certain extent, the film is autobiographical as Allen stars as Val Waxman, a 60ish director who saw his prime a decade ago. But unlike Allen, Val hasn't been able to direct a feature film in years. In fact, when he is first seen, Val is directing a deodorant commercial in snowy Canada, which he promptly quits to return to his ditzy and much younger girlfriend Lori (Debra Messing) in Manhattan. An aspiring actress, Lori is just waiting for Val -- whose neurotic and hypochondriac tendencies have earned him a bad reputation -- to land a picture so he can cast her in it. (Although audiences are familiar with Allen's penchant for casting himself in May-December romances in his films, this conceit becomes increasingly difficult to believe, especially when the grayer, wrinkled Allen is hooking up with women 30 years his junior.)

Just as Allen thinks he's hit bottom, his ex-wife Ellie (Tea Leoni), an executive with Galaxie Pictures recommends him as the perfect choice to direct the studio's upcoming $60 million period drama "The City That Never Sleeps." Although it takes some persuading her boss and fianc� Hal (Treat Williams) and Ed (George Hamilton), a studio hanger-on who walks around with a golf putty and whose job description is unclear, Val is offered the job.

What happens next is the nightmare of an visual artist: Val goes blind. His analyst explains that it is a psychosomatic response to pressure and heavy responsibility. But his agent, Al Hack (Mark Rydell) insists the show must go on. This leads to all kinds of subterfuge to keep the cast, crew and Hal -- who actually stole Ellie away from Val -- in the dark. Although this may have been a funny concept on paper, or even in a smaller dose, the film beats out every obvious joke, most of which are uninspired as Allen bumps into furniture, talks to walls and attempts to answer questions in the vaguest manner possible. Although a clever line or two does provide a good laugh, some of the ad-libbed dialogue seems forced. And the film could have also used a more disciplined editing hand as the film goes on too long.

Dire-hard fans of the Woodman may enjoy his recognizable comedic style and wit, but there's not much of it to make the film anything more than mildly amusing.

Due to a few sexual references and brief drug content, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.(
2002
)
